claim: In dopaminergic (DA) Substantia nigra (SN) neurons Cav2.3 R-type Ca2+-currents contribute to somatodendritic Ca2+-oscillations.
source: In dopaminergic (DA) Substantia nigra (SN) neurons Cav2.3 R-type Ca2+-currents contribute to somatodendritic Ca2+-oscillations.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Benkert et al., 2019) mentioned in the Introduction section.

claim: Cav2.3-knockout is neuroprotective in a PD mouse model.
source: This activity may contribute to the selective degeneration of these neurons in Parkinson's disease (PD) since Cav2.3-knockout is neuroprotective in a PD mouse model.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Benkert et al., 2019) mentioned in the Introduction section.

claim: In tsA-201-cells the membrane-anchored β2-splice variants β2a and β2e are required to stabilize Cav2.3 gating properties allowing sustained Cav2.3 availability during simulated pacemaking.
source: Here, we show that in tsA-201-cells the membrane-anchored β2-splice variants β2a and β2e are required to stabilize Cav2.3 gating properties allowing sustained Cav2.3 availability during simulated pacemaking and enhanced Ca2+-currents during bursts.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 1, 3, and 5 showing gating properties and current stability during pacemaking protocols.

claim: β2a and β2e enhance Ca2+-currents during bursts.
source: Here, we show that in tsA-201-cells the membrane-anchored β2-splice variants β2a and β2e are required to stabilize Cav2.3 gating properties allowing sustained Cav2.3 availability during simulated pacemaking and enhanced Ca2+-currents during bursts.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5 showing integrated Ca2+ currents during burst activity.

claim: β2a- and β2e-subunit transcripts are expressed in the mouse SN.
source: We confirmed the expression of β2a- and β2e-subunit transcripts in the mouse SN and in identified SN DA neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 2 and RNAscope data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: β2a- and β2e-subunit transcripts are expressed in identified SN DA neurons.
source: We confirmed the expression of β2a- and β2e-subunit transcripts in the mouse SN and in identified SN DA neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAscope data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and single-cell RT-qPCR data.

claim: Patch-clamp recordings of mouse DA midbrain neurons in culture revealed SNX-482-sensitive R-type Ca2+-currents with voltage-dependent gating properties that suggest modulation by β2a- and/or β2e-subunits.
source: Patch-clamp recordings of mouse DA midbrain neurons in culture and SN DA neurons in brain slices revealed SNX-482-sensitive R-type Ca2+-currents with voltage-dependent gating properties that suggest modulation by β2a- and/or β2e-subunits.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 7 showing voltage-dependent gating of SNX-482-sensitive currents in cultured neurons.

claim: Patch-clamp recordings of SN DA neurons in brain slices revealed SNX-482-sensitive R-type Ca2+-currents with voltage-dependent gating properties that suggest modulation by β2a- and/or β2e-subunits.
source: Patch-clamp recordings of mouse DA midbrain neurons in culture and SN DA neurons in brain slices revealed SNX-482-sensitive R-type Ca2+-currents with voltage-dependent gating properties that suggest modulation by β2a- and/or β2e-subunits.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 6 showing voltage-dependent gating of R-type and SNX-482-sensitive currents in brain slices.

claim: β-subunit alternative splicing may prevent a fraction of Cav2.3 channels from inactivation in continuously active, highly vulnerable SN DA neurons.
source: Thus, β-subunit alternative splicing may prevent a fraction of Cav2.3 channels from inactivation in continuously active, highly vulnerable SN DA neurons, thereby also supporting Ca2+ signals contributing to the (patho)physiological role of Cav2.3 channels in PD.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing β2a/β2e effects on channel inactivation and their expression in SN DA neurons.

claim: β-subunit alternative splicing supports Ca2+ signals contributing to the (patho)physiological role of Cav2.3 channels in PD.
source: Thus, β-subunit alternative splicing may prevent a fraction of Cav2.3 channels from inactivation in continuously active, highly vulnerable SN DA neurons, thereby also supporting Ca2+ signals contributing to the (patho)physiological role of Cav2.3 channels in PD.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data and previous findings about Cav2.3 in PD models.

claim: Parkinson's disease (PD) is one of the most common neurodegenerative disorders.
source: Parkinson's disease (PD) is one of the most common neurodegenerative disorders.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about PD.

claim: PD motor symptoms are characterized by progressive degeneration of dopamine (DA)-releasing neurons in the Substantia nigra (SN).
source: Its motor symptoms are characterized by progressive degeneration of dopamine (DA)-releasing neurons in the Substantia nigra (SN), while neighboring DA neurons in the ventral tegmental area (VTA) remain largely unaffected (Damier et al., 1999; Giguère et al., 2018; Surmeier et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Neighboring DA neurons in the ventral tegmental area (VTA) remain largely unaffected in PD.
source: Its motor symptoms are characterized by progressive degeneration of dopamine (DA)-releasing neurons in the Substantia nigra (SN), while neighboring DA neurons in the ventral tegmental area (VTA) remain largely unaffected (Damier et al., 1999; Giguère et al., 2018; Surmeier et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Current PD therapy is only symptomatic and primarily based on the substitution of striatal DA by administration of L-DOPA or dopamine D2 receptor agonists.
source: Current PD therapy is only symptomatic and primarily based on the substitution of striatal DA by administration of L-DOPA or dopamine D2 receptor agonists.
evidence: This is established knowledge about current PD treatment approaches.

claim: None of the existing therapeutic approaches for PD patients is disease-modifying and can prevent disease progression.
source: Unfortunately, none of the existing therapeutic approaches for PD patients is disease-modifying and can prevent disease progression (for review see Liss and Striessnig, 2019; Surmeier et al., 2011; Surmeier et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Elevated metabolic stress appears to play a central role in the high vulnerability of SN DA neurons.
source: Among these mechanisms, elevated metabolic stress appears to play a central role (for review see Liss and Striessnig, 2019), eventually triggering lysosomal, proteasomal and mitochondrial dysfunction (Burbulla et al., 2017; Surmeier et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Elevated metabolic stress eventually triggers lysosomal, proteasomal and mitochondrial dysfunction in SN DA neurons.
source: Among these mechanisms, elevated metabolic stress appears to play a central role (for review see Liss and Striessnig, 2019), eventually triggering lysosomal, proteasomal and mitochondrial dysfunction (Burbulla et al., 2017; Surmeier et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Increased cytosolic DA levels favor metabolic stress in SN DA neurons.
source: Intrinsic physiological properties of SN DA neurons, in particular increased cytosolic DA levels and high energy demand due to large axonal arborization favor metabolic stress (Bolam and Pissadaki, 2012; Liss and Striessnig, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: High energy demand due to large axonal arborization favors metabolic stress in SN DA neurons.
source: Intrinsic physiological properties of SN DA neurons, in particular increased cytosolic DA levels and high energy demand due to large axonal arborization favor metabolic stress (Bolam and Pissadaki, 2012; Liss and Striessnig, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SN DA neurons must handle a constant intracellular Ca2+-load resulting from dendritic and somatic Ca2+-oscillations triggered during their continuous electrical activity.
source: In addition, these neurons must handle a constant intracellular Ca2+-load resulting from dendritic and somatic Ca2+-oscillations triggered during their continuous electrical activity (Ortner et al., 2017; Surmeier et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Dendritic Ca2+-transients largely depend on the activity of voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, in particular Cav1.3 L-type (LTCCs) and T-type channels.
source: Dendritic Ca2+-transients largely depend on the activity of voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, in particular Cav1.3 L-type (LTCCs) and T-type channels (Guzman et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Cav1.3 channels can activate at subthreshold membrane potentials.
source: Cav1.3 channels can activate at subthreshold membrane potentials (Koschak et al., 2001; Lieb et al., 2014; Xu and Lipscombe, 2001) and do not completely inactivate during continuous pacemaking activity (Guzman et al., 2018; Guzman et al., 2009; Ortner et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cav1.3 channels do not completely inactivate during continuous pacemaking activity.
source: Cav1.3 channels can activate at subthreshold membrane potentials (Koschak et al., 2001; Lieb et al., 2014; Xu and Lipscombe, 2001) and do not completely inactivate during continuous pacemaking activity (Guzman et al., 2018; Guzman et al., 2009; Ortner et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Some in vivo studies showed neuroprotection by the systemic administration of dihydropyridine (DHP) LTCC blockers in 6-OHDA and MPTP animal models of PD.
source: Some, but not all, in vivo studies (Liss and Striessnig, 2019) showed neuroprotection by the systemic administration of dihydropyridine (DHP) LTCC blockers in 6-OHDA and MPTP animal models of PD thus further supporting a role of LTCCs as potential neuroprotective drug target.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: The STEADY-PD III trial reported no evidence for neuroprotection by isradipine (ISR).
source: This trial reported no evidence for neuroprotection by ISR.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the STEADY-PD III trial (Investigators, 2020).

claim: Only about 50% of the Ca2+-transients are blocked by ISR in the dendrites of SN DA neurons.
source: This is supported by the observation that only about 50% of the Ca2+-transients are blocked by ISR in the dendrites of SN DA neurons (Guzman et al., 2018) and that action potential-associated Ca2+-transients in the soma appear to be even resistant to ISR (Ortner et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Action potential-associated Ca2+-transients in the soma of SN DA neurons appear to be resistant to ISR.
source: This is supported by the observation that only about 50% of the Ca2+-transients are blocked by ISR in the dendrites of SN DA neurons (Guzman et al., 2018) and that action potential-associated Ca2+-transients in the soma appear to be even resistant to ISR (Ortner et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: SN DA neurons in mice lacking Cav2.3 channels were fully protected from neurodegeneration in the chronic MPTP-model of PD.
source: We have recently shown that SN DA neurons in mice lacking Cav2.3 channels were fully protected from neurodegeneration in the chronic MPTP-model of PD.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Benkert et al., 2019).

claim: Cav2.3 is the most abundant Cav expressed in SN DA neurons.
source: Moreover, we found that Cav2.3 is the most abundant Cav expressed in SN DA neurons, and substantially contributes to activity-related somatic Ca2+-oscillations (Benkert et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Benkert et al., 2019).

claim: Cav2.3 substantially contributes to activity-related somatic Ca2+-oscillations in SN DA neurons.
source: Moreover, we found that Cav2.3 is the most abundant Cav expressed in SN DA neurons, and substantially contributes to activity-related somatic Ca2+-oscillations (Benkert et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Benkert et al., 2019).

claim: SN DA neurons are spontaneously active, pacemaking neurons, either firing in a low-frequency single-spike mode or transiently in a high-frequency burst mode.
source: SN DA neurons are spontaneously active, pacemaking neurons, either firing in a low-frequency single-spike mode or transiently in a high-frequency burst mode (Grace and Bunney, 1984; Paladini and Roeper, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: During regular pacemaking the membrane potential of SN DA neurons is, on average, rather depolarized ranging from about –70 mV after an action potential (AP) to about –40 mV at firing threshold.
source: During regular pacemaking their membrane potential is, on average, rather depolarized ranging from about –70 mV after an action potential (AP) to about –40 mV at firing threshold (Gantz et al., 2018; Guzman et al., 2018; Ortner et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cav2.3 α1-subunits have originally been cloned as a low-voltage-gated channel with a negative steady-state inactivation voltage-range (V0.5,inact –78 mV).
source: However, Cav2.3 α1-subunits have originally been cloned as a low-voltage-gated channel with a negative steady-state inactivation voltage-range (V0.5,inact –78 mV; Soong et al., 1993) with almost complete inactivation at voltages positive to –50 mV.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: SNX-482-sensitive R-type currents mediated by Cav2.3 α1 subunits recorded from different neuronal cell types reveal a wide voltage-range of steady-state inactivation.
source: Interestingly, SNX-482-sensitive R-type currents mediated by Cav2.3 α1 subunits (Newcomb et al., 1998) recorded from different neuronal cell types reveal a wide voltage-range of steady-state inactivation despite similar recording conditions (5–10 mM Ba2+ as charge carrier): half-maximal voltages for steady-state inactivation (V0.5,inact) range from –90 to –70 mV in cerebellar, cortical and myenteric neurons (Bian et al., 2004; Sochivko et al., 2002; Tottene et al., 2000) to –58 mV in neurohypophyseal terminals (Wang et al., 1999) and to even as positive as –40 mV in GnRH-releasing neurons or GT1-7 cells (Kato et al., 2003; Watanabe et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Half-maximal voltages for steady-state inactivation (V0.5,inact) of SNX-482-sensitive R-type currents range from –90 to –70 mV in cerebellar, cortical and myenteric neurons.
source: Interestingly, SNX-482-sensitive R-type currents mediated by Cav2.3 α1 subunits (Newcomb et al., 1998) recorded from different neuronal cell types reveal a wide voltage-range of steady-state inactivation despite similar recording conditions (5–10 mM Ba2+ as charge carrier): half-maximal voltages for steady-state inactivation (V0.5,inact) range from –90 to –70 mV in cerebellar, cortical and myenteric neurons (Bian et al., 2004; Sochivko et al., 2002; Tottene et al., 2000) to –58 mV in neurohypophyseal terminals (Wang et al., 1999) and to even as positive as –40 mV in GnRH-releasing neurons or GT1-7 cells (Kato et al., 2003; Watanabe et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: V0.5,inact of SNX-482-sensitive R-type currents is –58 mV in neurohypophyseal terminals.
source: Interestingly, SNX-482-sensitive R-type currents mediated by Cav2.3 α1 subunits (Newcomb et al., 1998) recorded from different neuronal cell types reveal a wide voltage-range of steady-state inactivation despite similar recording conditions (5–10 mM Ba2+ as charge carrier): half-maximal voltages for steady-state inactivation (V0.5,inact) range from –90 to –70 mV in cerebellar, cortical and myenteric neurons (Bian et al., 2004; Sochivko et al., 2002; Tottene et al., 2000) to –58 mV in neurohypophyseal terminals (Wang et al., 1999) and to even as positive as –40 mV in GnRH-releasing neurons or GT1-7 cells (Kato et al., 2003; Watanabe et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: V0.5,inact of SNX-482-sensitive R-type currents is as positive as –40 mV in GnRH-releasing neurons or GT1-7 cells.
source: Interestingly, SNX-482-sensitive R-type currents mediated by Cav2.3 α1 subunits (Newcomb et al., 1998) recorded from different neuronal cell types reveal a wide voltage-range of steady-state inactivation despite similar recording conditions (5–10 mM Ba2+ as charge carrier): half-maximal voltages for steady-state inactivation (V0.5,inact) range from –90 to –70 mV in cerebellar, cortical and myenteric neurons (Bian et al., 2004; Sochivko et al., 2002; Tottene et al., 2000) to –58 mV in neurohypophyseal terminals (Wang et al., 1999) and to even as positive as –40 mV in GnRH-releasing neurons or GT1-7 cells (Kato et al., 2003; Watanabe et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Alternative splicing of Cav2.3 α1 subunits is unlikely to account for large shifts in steady-state inactivation.
source: While alternative splicing of Cav2.3 α1 subunits is unlikely to account for such large shifts in steady-state inactivation (Pereverzev et al., 2002), accessory β-subunits appear as obvious candidates for several reasons.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: β-subunits form part of the Cav2.3 channel complex and affect its membrane targeting and gating properties.
source: First, like for other high-voltage-activated Ca2+ channels (including Cav2.1 and Cav2.2, Liu et al., 1996; Scott et al., 1996) they form part of the Cav2.3 channel complex and thus affect its membrane targeting and gating properties (Zamponi et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: β-subunits tightly control V0.5,inact of Cav2 channels, including Cav2.3.
source: Second, previous work has shown that β-subunits tightly control V0.5,inact of Cav2 channels, including Cav2.3.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work on β-subunit modulation of calcium channels.

claim: All cytosolic β-subunit isoforms (β1 – β4 and cytosolic splice variants of β2) induce steady-state inactivation at negative potentials, being almost complete at voltages positive to –50 mV.
source: While all cytosolic β-subunit isoforms (β1 – β4 and cytosolic splice variants of β2) induce steady-state inactivation at negative potentials, being almost complete at voltages positive to –50 mV, the membrane-anchored β2 subunit splice variants β2a and β2e induce strong positive shifts of V0.5,inact of Cav2.3 channels and slow the time course of voltage-dependent inactivation (Jones et al., 1998; Pereverzev et al., 2002; Soong et al., 1993; Williams et al., 1994; Yasuda et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The membrane-anchored β2 subunit splice variants β2a and β2e induce strong positive shifts of V0.5,inact of Cav2.3 channels.
source: While all cytosolic β-subunit isoforms (β1 – β4 and cytosolic splice variants of β2) induce steady-state inactivation at negative potentials, being almost complete at voltages positive to –50 mV, the membrane-anchored β2 subunit splice variants β2a and β2e induce strong positive shifts of V0.5,inact of Cav2.3 channels and slow the time course of voltage-dependent inactivation (Jones et al., 1998; Pereverzev et al., 2002; Soong et al., 1993; Williams et al., 1994; Yasuda et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: β2a and β2e slow the time course of voltage-dependent inactivation of Cav2.3 channels.
source: While all cytosolic β-subunit isoforms (β1 – β4 and cytosolic splice variants of β2) induce steady-state inactivation at negative potentials, being almost complete at voltages positive to –50 mV, the membrane-anchored β2 subunit splice variants β2a and β2e induce strong positive shifts of V0.5,inact of Cav2.3 channels and slow the time course of voltage-dependent inactivation (Jones et al., 1998; Pereverzev et al., 2002; Soong et al., 1993; Williams et al., 1994; Yasuda et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: During simulated SN DA neuron-like continuous tonic pacemaking Cav2.3 channels remained active only when associated with β2a or β2e, but not the cytosolic β3 and β4 subunits.
source: When co-expressed together with auxiliary α2δ1-subunits in tsA-201 cells we indeed found that during simulated SN DA neuron-like continuous tonic pacemaking or brief burst activity (Ortner et al., 2017) Cav2.3 channels remained active only when associated with β2a or β2e, but not the cytosolic β3 and β4 subunits.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Steady-state inactivation of Cav1.3 channels was largely unaffected by β2a.
source: In contrast, steady-state inactivation of Cav1.3 channels was largely unaffected by β2a, suggesting that Cav1.3 availability is much less dependent on the presence of β2a subunits.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cav1.3 availability is much less dependent on the presence of β2a subunits.
source: In contrast, steady-state inactivation of Cav1.3 channels was largely unaffected by β2a, suggesting that Cav1.3 availability is much less dependent on the presence of β2a subunits.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing minimal effect of β2a on Cav1.3 inactivation.

claim: β2-subunits represent about 25% of all β-subunit transcripts in the mouse SN and VTA.
source: Using RNAscope we confirmed the presence of both β2a and β2e transcripts in identified mouse SN and VTA DA neurons and quantitative PCR analysis showed that β2-subunits represent about 25% of all β-subunit transcripts in the mouse SN and VTA with about 50% comprising β2a and β2e variants.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: About 50% of β2-subunit transcripts in the mouse SN and VTA comprise β2a and β2e variants.
source: Using RNAscope we confirmed the presence of both β2a and β2e transcripts in identified mouse SN and VTA DA neurons and quantitative PCR analysis showed that β2-subunits represent about 25% of all β-subunit transcripts in the mouse SN and VTA with about 50% comprising β2a and β2e variants.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: In patch-clamp recordings of SN DA neurons in mouse brain slices, SNX-482-sensitive R-type Ca2+-currents were detected with voltage-dependent inactivation properties suggesting a contribution of β2a- or β2e-stabilized Cav2.3-currents.
source: In patch-clamp recordings of SN DA neurons in mouse brain slices, we detected SNX-482-sensitive R-type Ca2+-currents with voltage-dependent inactivation properties suggesting a contribution of β2a- or β2e-stabilized Cav2.3-currents.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6.

claim: Recordings in cultured DA midbrain neurons confirmed R-type current activity during the pacemaking cycle.
source: Recordings in cultured DA midbrain neurons confirmed R-type current activity during the pacemaking cycle.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7.

claim: Cav2.3e is the only Cav2.3 α1-subunit splice variant detected in UV laser-microdissected mouse SN DA neurons.
source: Moreover, we specifically employed the Cav2.3e α1-subunit splice variant for our recordings, which among the six major Cav2.3 α1-subunit splice variants, was the only one detected in UV laser-microdissected mouse SN DA neurons in experiments using a qualitative single-cell RT-qPCR approach (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Recombinant Cav2.3 channels when associated with cytosolic β3 or β4 subunits inactivate at negative voltages (V0.5,inact < –70 mV).
source: In agreement with earlier studies (Jones et al., 1998; Yasuda et al., 2004), we found that recombinant Cav2.3 channels when associated with cytosolic β3 or β4 subunits inactivate at negative voltages (V0.5,inact < –70 mV) and with a rapid inactivation time course (≥50% within 50 ms, Figure 1B–C, Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1B-C and Table 1.

claim: Recombinant Cav2.3 channels when associated with cytosolic β3 or β4 subunits inactivate with a rapid inactivation time course (≥50% within 50 ms).
source: In agreement with earlier studies (Jones et al., 1998; Yasuda et al., 2004), we found that recombinant Cav2.3 channels when associated with cytosolic β3 or β4 subunits inactivate at negative voltages (V0.5,inact < –70 mV) and with a rapid inactivation time course (≥50% within 50 ms, Figure 1B–C, Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1B-C and Table 1.

claim: The cytosolic β2d splice variant shows a gating behavior very similar to β4.
source: The cytosolic β2d splice variant also showed a gating behavior very similar to β4.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1 and Table 1.

claim: β2a slowed the inactivation time course and shifted Cav2.3 voltage-dependent inactivation by ~30 mV to more positive potentials compared to β4.
source: In contrast, β2a, which is anchored to the plasma membrane through N-terminal palmitoylation, slowed the inactivation time course and shifted Cav2.3 voltage-dependent inactivation by ~30 mV to more positive potentials compared to β4 (and β3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1 and Table 1.

claim: With co-expressed β2e, gating properties were similar to β2a-containing Cav2.3 channel complexes.
source: Likewise, with co-expressed β2e, which is membrane anchored through N-terminal phospholipid interaction (Buraei and Yang, 2010; Miranda-Laferte et al., 2014), gating properties were similar to β2a-containing Cav2.3 channel complexes (Figure 1A–C, Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1A-C and Table 1.

claim: The shift in the voltage-dependence of inactivation by β2a was largely dependent on N-terminal palmitoylation.
source: In the case of β2a, the shift in the voltage-dependence of inactivation, but not the slowing of the inactivation time course, was largely dependent on N-terminal palmitoylation as shown with the palmitoylation-deficient mutant C3S/C4Sβ2a (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The slowing of the inactivation time course by β2a was not dependent on N-terminal palmitoylation.
source: In the case of β2a, the shift in the voltage-dependence of inactivation, but not the slowing of the inactivation time course, was largely dependent on N-terminal palmitoylation as shown with the palmitoylation-deficient mutant C3S/C4Sβ2a (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The voltage-dependence of activation was similar for all tested β-subunits.
source: The voltage-dependence of activation was similar for all tested β-subunits (Figure 1A, Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1A and Table 1.

claim: β2a and β2e subunits induce window currents at negative potentials.
source: Due to the voltage-dependent inactivation at more depolarized potentials and the resulting overlap of the steady-state activation and inactivation curves (Figure 1B), β2a and β2e subunits induce window currents, i.e. steady-state Ca2+ influx, at negative potentials (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1B and 1D.

claim: All five tested β-subunits (β2a, β2d, β2e, β3, β4) caused a robust and highly significant (6–12-fold) increase in current densities.
source: In our experiments, all five tested β-subunits (β2a, β2d, β2e, β3, β4) caused a robust and highly significant (6–12-fold; Figure 1A, Table 1) increase in current densities.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1A and Table 1.

claim: β-associated Cav2.3 channels contribute more to overall Cav2.3-mediated currents than channel complexes devoid of β-subunits.
source: This implies that β-associated Cav2.3 channels contribute more to overall Cav2.3-mediated currents than channel complexes devoid of β-subunits and thus can be subject to differential modulation by β-subunits.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing increased current densities with β-subunits.

claim: In both SN and VTA tissue, β4 (SN:~64%; VTA:~57%) and β2 (SN:~27%; VTA:~29%) represented the most abundant β-subunit transcripts.
source: In both SN and VTA tissue, β4 (SN:~64%; VTA:~57%) and β2 (SN:~27%; VTA:~29%) represented the most abundant β-subunit transcripts, followed by β1 and β3 (~4–7%) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: β1 and β3 comprise ~4–7% of β-subunit transcripts in SN and VTA tissue.
source: In both SN and VTA tissue, β4 (SN:~64%; VTA:~57%) and β2 (SN:~27%; VTA:~29%) represented the most abundant β-subunit transcripts, followed by β1 and β3 (~4–7%) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: RT-qPCR findings are in excellent agreement (β2: 31–35%, β4: 41–45%) with cell-type-specific RNA sequencing data from identified mouse midbrain DA neurons.
source: Our findings are in excellent agreement (β2: 31–35%, β4: 41–45%) with cell-type-specific RNA sequencing data from identified mouse midbrain DA neurons (Brichta et al., 2015; Shin, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with published RNA sequencing data.

claim: In SN and VTA, β2a (~30%) and β2e (~26%) transcripts together comprised about half of all tested β2-subunit splice variants.
source: In SN and VTA, β2a (~30%) and β2e (~26%) transcripts together comprised about half of all tested β2-subunit splice variants, cytosolic β2c and β2d-species about 42% and β2b only about 3% (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: Cytosolic β2c and β2d-species comprise about 42% of β2-subunit splice variants in SN and VTA.
source: In SN and VTA, β2a (~30%) and β2e (~26%) transcripts together comprised about half of all tested β2-subunit splice variants, cytosolic β2c and β2d-species about 42% and β2b only about 3% (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: β2b comprises only about 3% of β2-subunit splice variants in SN and VTA.
source: In SN and VTA, β2a (~30%) and β2e (~26%) transcripts together comprised about half of all tested β2-subunit splice variants, cytosolic β2c and β2d-species about 42% and β2b only about 3% (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: With co-expressed β3 and β4 isoforms simulated SN DA neuron regular pacemaker activity induced large inward currents in response to single AP waveforms.
source: With co-expressed β3 and β4 isoforms simulated SN DA neuron regular pacemaker activity (initiated from a holding potential of –89 mV) induced large inward currents in response to single AP waveforms (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Cav2.3 channels conducted ICa during the repolarization phase of the AP without evidence for inward current during the interspike interval (ISI) when co-expressed with β3 or β4.
source: Cav2.3 channels conducted ICa during the repolarization phase of the AP (IAP) without evidence for inward current during the interspike interval (ISI, Figure 3A and B bottom inset).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3A and B.

claim: IAP decreased rapidly during continuous activity and almost completely disappeared after 1 (co-transfected β3)–2 min (co-transfected β4) during simulated pacemaking.
source: However, IAP decreased rapidly during continuous activity and almost completely disappeared after 1 (co-transfected β3)–2 min (co-transfected β4; Figure 3A, B, E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3A, B, E and F.

claim: Cav2.3e α1-subunits, in complex with α2δ1 and β3 or β4, cannot support substantial inward currents during continuous SN DA neuron pacemaking activity.
source: Our data, therefore, suggest that Cav2.3e α1-subunits, in complex with α2δ1 and β3 or β4, cannot support substantial inward currents during continuous SN DA neuron pacemaking activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing rapid current decay with β3 and β4.

claim: About 40% of the maximal initial IAP remained even after 5 min of continuous activity with β2a or β2e.
source: When analyzed in parallel under identical experimental conditions IAP decreased with a much slower time course with about 40% of the maximal initial IAP still remaining even after 5 min of continuous activity (Figure 3C–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3C-F.

claim: β2a or β2e supported Cav2.3 ICa predominantly during the repolarization phase after the AP spike.
source: Similar to co-transfected β3 or β4 subunits, β2a or β2e supported Cav2.3 ICa predominantly during the repolarization phase after the AP spike.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3C and D.

claim: β2a and β2e also supported an inward current during the interspike interval (ISI).
source: However, in accordance with enhanced window currents at negative voltages (Figure 1D) these subunits also supported an inward current during the interspike interval (ISI) as evident from the first few sweeps (with the largest current amplitudes) (Figure 3C and D, bottom insets).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3C and D and Figure 1D.

claim: IAP persisting after 2 min (β3, β4) or 5 min (β2a, β2e) of pacemaking was completely blocked by 100 µM Cd2+ with almost complete recovery upon washout.
source: IAP persisting after 2 min (β3, β4) or 5 min (β2a, β2e) of pacemaking was completely blocked by 100 µM Cd2+ with almost complete recovery upon washout (Figure 3A–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3A-E.

claim: β3 co-transfected Cav2.3 channels showed a time-dependent current run-down to about 60% of the peak ICa after 5 min during 0.1 Hz square pulse protocol.
source: While β3 co-transfected Cav2.3 channels showed a time-dependent current run-down to about 60% of the peak ICa after 5 min, β2a prevented the current decline during this period (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4A.

claim: β2a prevented the current decline during 5 min of 0.1 Hz square pulse protocol.
source: While β3 co-transfected Cav2.3 channels showed a time-dependent current run-down to about 60% of the peak ICa after 5 min, β2a prevented the current decline during this period (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4A.

claim: After 30 s of pacemaking the current amplitude during the first AP after the pause was similar to IAP during the initial AP with both β3 and β2a subunits.
source: After 30 s of pacemaking the current amplitude during the first AP after the pause was similar to IAP during the initial AP with both β-subunits (β3: 96.9% ± 3.63%, 95% CI: 86.8–107.0, n=5, N=2; β2a: 107.3% ± 3.66%, 95% CI: 99.3–115.4, n=12, N=2, of the initial IAP).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4B.

claim: After 4.5 min total pacemaking, recovery decreased to 54.7% ± 6.27% with co-transfected β3.
source: After the pause that followed another 1 min of pacemaking, 83.6% ± 7.33% (95% CI: 63.2–103.9) of the initial current was still recovered with co-transfected β3 but after 2 more minutes of pacemaking recovery decreased to 54.7% ± 6.27% (95% CI: 34.7–74.7, Figure 4B;~45% run-down after 4.5 min in total, n=5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4B.

claim: Run-down was largely prevented by co-expressed β2a-subunits (~16% run-down after 4.5 min in total).
source: Again, run-down was largely prevented by co-expressed β2a-subunits (Figure 4B;~16% run-down after 4.5 min in total, n=12).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4B.

claim: The IAP decrease in response to simulated SN DA neuron pacemaking (2.5 Hz) is almost completely due to the reversible accumulation of Cav2.3 channels in inactivated states.
source: These data clearly demonstrate that the IAP decrease in response to simulated SN DA neuron pacemaking (2.5 Hz) is almost completely due to the reversible accumulation of Cav2.3 channels in inactivated states, an effect partially prevented by β2a and β2e.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing recovery after pauses and Cd2+ block.

claim: Integrated ICa during the burst was four- to sixfold higher than the mean integrated ICa during a steady-state AP with all co-expressed β-subunits (β2a, β2e, β4).
source: Integrated ICa during the burst was four- to sixfold higher than the mean integrated ICa during a steady-state AP with all co-expressed β-subunits (β2a, β2e, β4) (Figure 5B, left panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5B.

claim: About 30% of currents recovered after 1.5 s at –89 mV with both co-expressed β4 and β2a in square-pulse recovery protocol.
source: About 30% of currents recovered under these experimental conditions after 1.5 s at –89 mV with both co-expressed β4 and β2a (~sixfold increase of the remaining ICa after 1 s at Vmax).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5C and Table 2.

claim: Recovery during the hyperpolarizing pause after the burst of the AP protocol was much less pronounced (β4) or absent (β2a, β2e).
source: In contrast, recovery during the hyperpolarizing pause after the burst of the AP protocol was much less pronounced (β4) or absent (β2a, β2e; Figure 5B, right panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5B.

claim: 100 nM SNX-482 inhibit ~30% of total Cav currents in mouse SN DA neurons when stimulated from a negative holding potential of –70 mV.
source: We have recently shown in whole-cell patch-clamp recordings that 100 nM SNX-482 inhibit ~30% of total Cav currents in mouse SN DA neurons (Benkert et al., 2019) when stimulated from a negative holding potential of –70 mV.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: R-type current evoked from –100 mV activated at ~8 mV more positive voltages than total ICa in SN DA neurons.
source: R-type current evoked from –100 mV activated at ~8 mV more positive voltages than total ICa (Figure 6A, Table 3 for statistics).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6A and Table 3.

claim: SNX-482-sensitive current steady-state inactivation was observed at significantly more positive voltages as compared to control current (–44.6 mV vs. –52.9 mV) in SN DA neurons.
source: Although the slope of the voltage-dependence of activation was different for the SNX-482-sensitive current as compared to R-type current, steady-state inactivation was again observed at significantly more positive voltages as compared to control current (–44.6 mV vs. –52.9 mV, Figure 6B, Table 3), and ~5 mV more negative than recombinant Cav2.3 currents associated with β4 or β3 (Table 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6B and Table 3.

claim: SNX-482-sensitive current V0.5,inact was ~5 mV more negative than recombinant Cav2.3 currents associated with β4 or β3.
source: Although the slope of the voltage-dependence of activation was different for the SNX-482-sensitive current as compared to R-type current, steady-state inactivation was again observed at significantly more positive voltages as compared to control current (–44.6 mV vs. –52.9 mV, Figure 6B, Table 3), and ~5 mV more negative than recombinant Cav2.3 currents associated with β4 or β3 (Table 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of experimental data in Figure 6B, Table 3 and Table 1.

claim: About 13% of the total ICa was inhibited by acute bath application of SNX-482 at holding potential of –60 mV in perforated patch recordings.
source: Indeed, under these conditions still about 13% of the total ICa was inhibited by acute bath application of SNX-482 and inhibition was partially reversible upon washout (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-D, Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-D.

claim: About 10% of current were blocked reversibly by the L-type channel blocker nifedipine (10 µM) at holding potential of –60 mV in perforated patch recordings.
source: Under these conditions, about 10% of current were blocked reversibly by the L-type channel blocker nifedipine (10 µM, Figure 6—figure supplement 1E-H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E-H.

claim: 100 nM SNX-482 significantly reduced non-LTCC currents by 41% ± 4% in primary cultures of mouse DA midbrain neurons.
source: When added after the complete block of LTCC currents by 3 µM isradipine (comprising 24.7% ± 4.2% of total Ca2+-current, n=15), 100 nM SNX-482 significantly reduced non-LTCC currents by 41% ± 4% (95% CI: 33–49, n=20, N=4, paired Student's t-test; P<0.001) (Figure 7A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7A-D.

claim: LTCC currents comprise 24.7% ± 4.2% of total Ca2+-current in primary cultures of mouse DA midbrain neurons.
source: When added after the complete block of LTCC currents by 3 µM isradipine (comprising 24.7% ± 4.2% of total Ca2+-current, n=15), 100 nM SNX-482 significantly reduced non-LTCC currents by 41% ± 4% (95% CI: 33–49, n=20, N=4, paired Student's t-test; P<0.001) (Figure 7A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7A-D.

claim: SNX-482-sensitive currents activated with a half maximal activation voltage (V0.5,act –9.2±0.6 mV) slightly more positive than non-LTCC current (V0.5,inact = -12.5 ± 0.6 mV) in cultured DA neurons.
source: SNX-482-sensitive currents (blue) activated with a half maximal activation voltage (V0.5,act –9.2±0.6 mV) slightly more positive than non-LTCC current (V0.5,inact = -12.5 ± 0.6 mV).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7E.

claim: SNX-482-sensitive current inactivation was best fit with a V0.5,inact of –58.1±0.6 mV in cultured DA neurons.
source: SNX-482-sensitive current inactivation was best fit with a V0.5,inact of –58.1±0.6 mV, which was 12–18 mV more positive than recombinant Cav2.3 currents expressed with β4 or β3 (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7F.

claim: SNX-482-sensitive current V0.5,inact was 12–18 mV more positive than recombinant Cav2.3 currents expressed with β4 or β3.
source: SNX-482-sensitive current inactivation was best fit with a V0.5,inact of –58.1±0.6 mV, which was 12–18 mV more positive than recombinant Cav2.3 currents expressed with β4 or β3 (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of experimental data in Figure 7F and Table 1.

claim: 100 nM SNX-482 significantly reduced the spontaneous firing frequency from 4.1±0.8 Hz to 1.1±0.2 Hz in cultured midbrain neurons.
source: In current-clamp recordings 100 nM SNX-482 significantly reduced the spontaneous firing frequency from 4.1±0.8 Hz (control, n=10, N=3; 95% CI: 2.1–6.1) to 1.1±0.2 Hz (SNX-482, n=10, 95% CI: 0.2–2.1, p=0.0036, paired Student's t-test; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, B), decreased the regularity of pacemaking and also caused changes in AP shape (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: 100 nM SNX-482 decreased the regularity of pacemaking in cultured midbrain neurons.
source: In current-clamp recordings 100 nM SNX-482 significantly reduced the spontaneous firing frequency from 4.1±0.8 Hz (control, n=10, N=3; 95% CI: 2.1–6.1) to 1.1±0.2 Hz (SNX-482, n=10, 95% CI: 0.2–2.1, p=0.0036, paired Student's t-test; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, B), decreased the regularity of pacemaking and also caused changes in AP shape (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: 100 nM SNX-482 caused changes in AP shape in cultured midbrain neurons.
source: In current-clamp recordings 100 nM SNX-482 significantly reduced the spontaneous firing frequency from 4.1±0.8 Hz (control, n=10, N=3; 95% CI: 2.1–6.1) to 1.1±0.2 Hz (SNX-482, n=10, 95% CI: 0.2–2.1, p=0.0036, paired Student's t-test; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, B), decreased the regularity of pacemaking and also caused changes in AP shape (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: Cav2.3-mediated currents may contribute to the pacemaking cycle in cultured DA neurons.
source: Cav2.3-mediated currents may therefore also contribute to the pacemaking cycle in cultured DA neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the effects of SNX-482 on pacemaking.

claim: The large shift of V0.5,inact of Cav2.3 R-type current by membrane-anchored β2a and β2e subunits would predict that Cav2.3 channel availability can be adjusted along a wide range of potentials (about 30 mV; V0.5,inact –40 to –70 mV).
source: The large shift of V0.5,inact of Cav2.3 R-type current by membrane-anchored β2a and β2e subunits would predict that Cav2.3 channel availability can be adjusted along a wide range of potentials (about 30 mV; V0.5,inact –40 to –70 mV, Table 1) just by varying the abundance and local availability of these subunits relative to cytosolic β-subunits within a cell or nanodomain.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing β-subunit effects on inactivation.

claim: Transcriptomic analysis of laser-captured SN DA neurons from 18 human postmortem brains shows 30% β2, 45% β4, 15% β3, 8% β1.
source: These data are in excellent agreement with RNAseq data from mouse midbrain DA neurons with expression levels of about 33% for β2% and 43% for β4 (Brichta et al., 2015; Shin, 2015) and transcriptomic analysis of laser-captured SN DA neurons from 18 human postmortem brains (30% β2, 45% β4; 15% β3, 8% β1; Aguila et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published transcriptomic data.

claim: β4-subunits may extensively target to channels at axonal presynaptic locations or to the nucleus.
source: For example, β4-subunits may extensively target to channels at axonal presynaptic locations (as reported in cultured hippocampal neurons) or even to the nucleus (where they regulate gene transcription) and thus contribute less to Cav2.3 channel complexes at somatodendritic sites (Etemad et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Differences in the affinity of β-subunits for their α1-subunit interaction domain in the I-II-linker may support preferential association with β2.
source: Moreover, differences in the affinity of β-subunits for their α1-subunit interaction domain in the I-II-linker may also support preferential association with β2 (De Waard et al., 1995).
evidence: This is speculation based on citation to previous literature.

claim: Cav2.3-knockout mice are protected from the selective loss of SN DA neurons in the chronic MPTP/probenecid PD model.
source: We have previously shown that Cav2.3-knockout mice are protected from the selective loss of SN DA neurons in the chronic MPTP/probenecid PD model (Benkert et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of Cav2.3 alone or together with other Cavs may confer beneficial disease-modifying effects and a novel approach for neuroprotection in PD.
source: Pharmacological inhibition of Cav2.3 alone or together with other Cavs may therefore confer beneficial disease-modifying effects and a novel approach for neuroprotection in PD.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental findings and previous work.

claim: The inhibition of Cav2.3 in addition to Cav1.3 may be required for clinically meaningful neuroprotection in PD.
source: Therefore, the inhibition of Cav2.3 in addition to Cav1.3 may be required for clinically meaningful neuroprotection.
evidence: This is speculation based on the failure of ISR in clinical trials and preclinical findings.

claim: Cav2.3-mediated R-type currents are notoriously drug-resistant.
source: However, Cav2.3-mediated R-type currents are notoriously drug-resistant (Schneider et al., 2013), and so far no selective potent small-molecule Cav2.3/R-type blocker has been reported.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: No selective potent small-molecule Cav2.3/R-type blocker has been reported.
source: However, Cav2.3-mediated R-type currents are notoriously drug-resistant (Schneider et al., 2013), and so far no selective potent small-molecule Cav2.3/R-type blocker has been reported.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the current state of Cav2.3 pharmacology.

claim: A neuroprotective strategy could aim at reducing Cav2.3 contribution to R-type current by interfering with the association of β2a and β2e subunits.
source: Rather than inhibiting Ca2+-entry through the pore-forming α1-subunit, such a strategy could aim at reducing its contribution to the R-type current component persisting during continuous activity in SN DA neurons by interfering with the association of β2a and β2e subunits.
evidence: This is speculation about potential therapeutic strategies based on the findings.

claim: CaVablator has been used to specifically target Ca2+-channel β-subunits for degradation by fusing β-specific nanobodies with the catalytic HECT domain of Nedd4L.
source: One such approach (CaVablator) has elegantly been used to specifically target Ca2+-channel β-subunits for degradation by fusing β-specific nanobodies with the catalytic HECT domain of Nedd4L, an E3 ubiquitin ligase (Morgenstern et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: CaVablator strongly reduces Cav1- and Cav2-mediated Ca2+-currents in different cell types.
source: This strongly reduces Cav1- and Cav2-mediated Ca2+-currents in different cell types.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Morgenstern et al., 2019).

claim: Cav2.3 α1-subunit (Cacna1e) transcripts are the most abundant α1-subunit expressed in mature SN DA neurons.
source: However, our recent quantitative RNAscope analyses in mature SN DA neurons (Benkert et al., 2019) clearly demonstrate that Cav2.3 α1-subunit (Cacna1e) transcripts are the most abundant α1-subunit expressed in these cells, in excellent agreement with cell-type-specific RNAseq data of identified midbrain DA neurons (Brichta et al., 2015; Shin, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: SNX-482 is a potent blocker of Kv4.3 channels underlying A-type K+-currents (IA).
source: While SNX-482 is highly suitable to isolate Cav2.3-mediated Ca2+ current components, effects on pacemaking also must take into account that this toxin is also a potent blocker of Kv4.3 channels (Kimm and Bean, 2014) underlying A-type K+-currents (IA).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: 60 nM SNX-482 nearly fully block reconstituted Kv4.3 currents in HEK cells (IC50 ~3 nM).
source: 60 nM nearly fully block reconstituted Kv4.3 currents in HEK cells (IC50 ~3 nM).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Kimm and Bean, 2014).

claim: Block of IA channels typically induces a broadening of APs in several neuronal preparations.
source: However, the observed SNX-482-induced shortening of APs and the reduction of spontaneous firing are difficult to reconcile with a block of IA channels, which typically induces a broadening of APs in several neuronal preparations (Kim et al., 2005) and an increased frequency in DA neurons (Liss et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Block of IA channels induces an increased frequency in DA neurons.
source: However, the observed SNX-482-induced shortening of APs and the reduction of spontaneous firing are difficult to reconcile with a block of IA channels, which typically induces a broadening of APs in several neuronal preparations (Kim et al., 2005) and an increased frequency in DA neurons (Liss et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In brain slices of Cav2.3 knockout mice, small changes in AP spike waveforms were observed, without major changes in pacemaking activity.
source: In brain slices of Cav2.3 knockout mice, small changes in AP spike waveforms were observed, without major changes in pacemaking activity (Benkert et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.
